# Selection — TRD §15 row 10: the terminal and portable cutover package formats

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 10 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §14.2, §14.4, §14.1, §9.3, §13.5, §13.8 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/package.json`](../../test/vectors/package.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-package-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-package-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md) added the fifth thing the package must carry and
supplies this row's reasoning a second time; [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md) is the largest part;
[row 8](./row-8-attribution-record.md) **deleted** a part; [row 14](./row-14-recovery-code.md) is where the
whole thing terminates; [row 6](./row-6-antireplay-retention.md) sets one part's depth.
**Amended by:** [`S0-5`](../review/remediation/S0-5/README.md) (2026-08-27) — a package carries checkpoints, so it carries their admissions. An importer re-derives
coverage locally and reads `self_admitted` rather than discarding it; the package's own shape is unchanged.

---

## The selection

```
ONE format, at THREE lineage states — not two formats             §13.5

  never established   §9.3's fidelity archive of a Local workspace
  live                §14.2's portable cutover package
  retired             §14.4's terminal package

  A live package is UPGRADED to a retired one by importing the
  terminal record. It is not replaced.

The parts

  checkpoint    row 7's ciphertext and manifest — row 8's attribution
                claims are INSIDE it, so there is no attribution part
  epochs        enough signed authorization history          §14.2 item 2
  suffix        envelopes after the checkpoint, to row 6's depth
  generations   the historical content keys, wrapped         §14.2 item 4
  head          the signed live head, or the terminal record §14.2 item 5
  recovery      R_pub and the code-sealed R_priv                  row 14

The manifest, signed by the assembler

  P = LP("done/pkg/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id)
      || LP(lineage_state) || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(hex lineage_head_digest)
      || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex parts_digest) || LP(assembled_by)

  parts_digest = SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-parts/v1")
                   || for each part ASCENDING BY NAME:
                        LP(name) || LP(dec count) || LP(hex digest) )

  No separate part count. Each part's count is already in the digest.

The trust-root anchor — the only thing here that is not an encoding

  Every generation is wrapped to R_pub with HPKE base mode, and its
  info binds the lineage the wrap was made under:

  info = LP("done/gen-wrap/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id)
         || LP(hex auth_root) || LP(dec gen)

  A substituted root derives a different key schedule, so the wrap
  opens nothing, so there is no content to re-attribute.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. §15 asked for two formats and there is one, and the TRD had already said so

The row is titled _terminal-package and portable cutover-package formats_, and reads as two artifacts to
design. Written side by side they are the same list, and §14.4 is not describing a second artifact at all:

> Every participating replica **and the verified portable package** receive that record plus `R_pub`, the
> code-sealed `R_priv`, enough public authorization history, verification keys, accepted-set evidence and
> recovery wraps for every generation…

That is the service **populating the portable package** before deletion. And the sentence three paragraphs
later closes it:

> It keeps its last signed **live** head — stale, but sufficient… Importing the package later upgrades its
> knowledge.

_Upgrades_, not _replaces_. So a package holds whichever of the two signed lineage objects exists, and
importing a terminal record moves a live package to retired. That is §13.5's state machine, which already has
exactly these states and an ancestor rule to move between them — and the third state, _never established_, is
§9.3's fidelity archive of a Local workspace, whose stated contents are the same list minus the parts a
lineage would have supplied.

**One format, one importer, one verifier, three states.** The saving is not the format count: it is that
§11.3's tests 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 exercise one code path, and that the state a device is looking at is a field it
reads rather than a shape it infers from which parts are present.

**§9.3 gets a consequence it should not be read past.** A Local archive has no lineage, so both anchor fields
are empty and `auth_root` names the archiving device. Nothing external authenticates it — and §9.3 already
says the archive answers _does ciphertext still exist_ and never _can you decrypt it_. The format does not
pretend otherwise, and the never-established vector is published so that the difference is visible rather than
described.

---

## 2. The trust-root anchor, which is the actual work

§14.2 item 1 is one clause with a whole problem inside it:

> An authenticated old trust root — the vanished service's authorization signing key, **bound so it cannot be
> substituted**. Otherwise whoever can write the archive can rewrite who wrote what.

**Every link below the root is service-signed, so a forger who supplies their own root can re-sign all of it.**
The epochs verify under `K_auth`. The credentials come from the epochs. Row 8's attribution claims verify under
the credentials. Substitute `K_auth` and re-issue the lot, and the package is internally consistent and says
whatever the forger wants about who wrote what. A signature over the package does not help: it is signed by
something the same substitution replaces.

**So the chain has to terminate in material the user holds, and there is exactly one such thing.** The
recovery code (row 14) opens `R_priv`. `R_priv` opens the generation wraps. So bind the trust root where the
wrap is made:

```
code  →  R_priv  →  a generation wrap whose info binds the root
      →  the content key  →  the content root  →  row 8's claims
      →  the credentials that signed them, resolved through epochs the root verifies
```

A forger has three moves and each fails on the same step:

| The forgery                                    | What happens                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Substitute the root and re-sign the history    | The wraps' `info` binds the real root, so **no generation opens** |
| Keep the real root, re-sign the history anyway | The history does not verify under the root the wraps demand       |
| Supply their own `R_pub` and their own wraps   | The code does not open their `R_priv` — row 14, unchanged         |

**The cost is two fields in an `info` that had none specified, and that is the whole selection.** No new key,
no new signature scheme, no new secret, and row 14's envelope is untouched.

**Bound in `info` rather than in the AEAD's AAD, deliberately.** `info` is never transmitted; both sides
construct it from context. So a reader must **supply** the root it believes and a wrong belief fails to open,
where an AAD would let the reader take the root out of the package and fail only to match. Row 11 bound its
transcript hash in an HPKE `info` for the same reason, and this is that argument at a second carrier.

**Per generation, which §14.1 makes correct rather than convenient.** Migration establishes a new lineage and
rotates to a fresh generation, so generations written before it stay anchored to the root that was in force
when they were written — which is exactly the root their attribution should be verified against. A per-package
binding would have had to choose one root for material written under two.

---

## 3. The anchor is only needed by one reader, and that is row 9's argument a fourth time

Row 9 interrogated _brand-new_ and found two of three arrival paths were not. The same interrogation applies
here, and it is why this row is small:

| Who is reading the package            | Where its trust root comes from                      |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| A surviving device                    | Its own enrollment. It has known `K_auth` for months |
| A device enrolled through row 11      | Through the person — the transcript binds the head   |
| **Recovery with no surviving device** | **Nowhere else. This is the reader that asks**       |

And the reader that asks is exactly the reader that must hold the recovery code, because §13.8 makes the code
the mandatory floor for content-key access and there is no account without one. **The anchor and the audience
for it arrive together**, which is what makes the construction available at all rather than a chicken-and-egg.

Row 9 wrote this about a signed head; §14.2 then owed a fifth item because of it. This row is where that item
lands as a part, and the reasoning turns out to cover the trust root as well.

---

## 4. Row 8 deleted a part, and that is where the saving actually came from

An earlier reading of §14.2 item 3 — _either the original signed envelopes or a validated
attribution-preserving checkpoint_ — implied an attribution part with its own digest, its own retention rule
and its own question of what to do when it disagrees with the snapshot beside it.

**Row 8 put the claims in the content root, so they are inside the checkpoint the package already carries.**
The part, the disagreement and the rule all stop existing. §7.6 had already required exactly this — attribution
evidence is _portable workspace material, checkpointed and restored with the workspace rather than held in a
separate channel_ — and this is the row where that sentence is collected rather than restated.

§14.2 item 4, the historical content-key generations, is **not** deleted by row 8 and it is worth being exact
about why. Row 8 closed the _attribution_ retention floor: verifying who wrote a card no longer needs the
generation that sealed its envelope, because §6.1's trim re-seals the claim forward. What the package still
needs generations for is **opening the ciphertext it carries** — the checkpoint under its generation, and any
earlier generation the suffix uses. That is §6.1's local-store retention question, which §13.7 already warns
must not be conflated with the other one, and it is bounded by the checkpoint rather than by history.

---

## 5. The parts digest, and the count field that is not there

```
parts_digest = SHA-256( LP("done/pkg-parts/v1")
                 || for each part ASCENDING BY NAME:
                      LP(name) || LP(dec count) || LP(hex digest) )
```

**The sort is row 7's canonicalization rule at a second carrier**, for the same reason: two devices assembling
a package over the same material must produce the same digest, and a map in insertion order would not.

**There is no separate part count in the manifest, and its absence is a decision.** Each part's own count is
inside this digest, so truncating a part and dropping one entirely both move it. A second count field would
restate a fact already bound and introduce the possibility of the two disagreeing — and a verifier facing a
disagreement between two bindings of the same fact has no principled answer.

That has a consequence for the vectors worth naming, because it is the rule this project adopted after row 13:
**a real truncation changes two things at once** — a count and the digest over it — so it cannot be an
isolating negative. It is published as a demonstration that both shapes move the digest, and the isolating
negative changes the digest alone.

---

## 6. Who signs, and the one state where nothing certifies the signer

`assembled_by` names the assembler and the manifest is signed by it. Three cases, one rule:

| State             | Assembler                | Resolved against                         |
| ----------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| live              | the restoring credential | the epochs the package carries           |
| retired           | the service              | the trust root itself (§14.4 commits it) |
| never established | the archiving device     | **nothing** — and §9.3 already says so   |

The rule is: **the assembler must be resolvable from the epochs the package carries, or be the trust root
itself, or — where there is no lineage — be the device that made the archive.** The third is not a weaker form
of the first two. There is no authority to appeal to for a workspace that never had one, and what authenticates
a Local archive is the code that opens it. The signature is integrity within something you have already
opened, which is worth having and is not worth describing as more.

All three are published as vectors, under two different signing keys, so the shapes are compared rather than
asserted.

---

## 7. What it costs

| Cost                           | Size                                                                           |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Per package                    | One Ed25519 signature, one SHA-256 over the sorted part list                   |
| Per generation                 | Two fields in an HPKE `info` — **no ciphertext grows**                         |
| Verification, brand-new reader | One HPKE open, then one signature per epoch it needs                           |
| New keys                       | **None**                                                                       |
| New signature schemes          | **None.** Ed25519, row 1                                                       |
| Changes to row 14              | **None.** The code-sealed `R_priv` envelope is untouched                       |
| Bundle                         | HPKE was already row 1's suite and row 11's dependency                         |
| Formats deleted                | One — §15 asked for two packages, and §9.3's archive folds in as a third state |

---

## 8. What this changes elsewhere

**§14.2 gains a stated anchor** where it had a requirement, and §13.7's rotation gains the `info` its wraps had
never been given.

**§9.3's fidelity archive stops being a separate artifact**, and one input to an open question moves with it.
[sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §5.4 weighs migrating the first deployment through the archive instead of
through Markdown, and prices that as _pulls a Stage 5 item into Stage 2_. That price is now smaller than it was
written: the archive is one state of a format Stage 4 has to build regardless, so the marginal cost is the
never-established state and an export path rather than a whole artifact. **That does not decide §5.4** — it is
an input, the question is the author's, and the other half of it is about attribution rather than cost.

**Not in this row.** How deep the suffix part reaches is [row 6](./row-6-antireplay-retention.md)'s. What the
service must do before deletion, and the catch-up window §14.4 requires, is Stage 4's. The escrow split of
§13.8 is a separate seal of `R_priv` and touches nothing here.

---

## 9. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-package-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check`
now runs it with the other twelve.

**Three vectors — one per lineage state — and fifteen negatives.** The three are the point of the row made
concrete: the same manifest construction at live, retired and never-established, signed by a credential, by the
service, and by an archiving device.

**Five negatives are the wrap's `info`, and `substituted-trust-root` is the row.** A forger's authorization key
offered in the root's place, and the generation wrap opens nothing.

**HPKE is implemented here rather than pinned as a string.** Row 11 pinned only its `info` and said so, because
its claim was about the transcript rather than the seal. This row's claim **is** a binding inside the seal, so
a pinned string would be the claim asserted rather than tested — and the coverage audit could not reach it. The
generator therefore carries RFC 9180 base mode over DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) and **reproduces RFC 9180 A.1.1
before it is used for anything**, on every invocation: encapsulation, decapsulation, the key schedule and the
ciphertext. A.1.1 is an AES-128-GCM vector while this suite is AES-256-GCM, which is the reason to run it
rather than a reason not to — the AEAD identifier is inside `suite_id`, so reproducing it exercises every
label, length prefix and step of the schedule, and the only thing it leaves unchecked is the constant this file
passes for its own AEAD.

**Every published keypair proves it is one keypair first**, including the X25519 one derived from RFC 7748
§6.1's scalar — row 14's rule, since a binding between a public key and a private one proves nothing if the
vector's own halves are unrelated.
